# Chat Completion {#sec-app-chat-completion}

Chat completion is the interface that turned a next-token model into a
product surface. This chapter explains how it got the shape it has: why a
flat completion API grew a role-structured message format, why the chat
abstraction won, and what the format gives up. By the end a reader can
explain why the chat interface looks the way it does.

## Problem

A raw language model completes text. A product needs a stable contract:
who said what, where the system's instructions end and the user's begin,
and how to stream a response token by token under a latency budget.

## Design

A message list with roles (system, user, assistant) over the completion
model, plus a streaming protocol. The model still predicts tokens; the API
imposes structure on the prompt and the response.

## Evolution

From raw text completion, to instruction-tuned completion, to the
role-structured chat format popularized by the chat completion APIs. Trace
why instruction tuning and RLHF made the chat surface viable, and how the
format became a de facto standard.

## Trade-offs

Roles add structure but blur under prompt injection, since everything is
still tokens. Templates pin behavior but fragment across providers.
Streaming improves perceived latency but complicates moderation and
cancellation.

## In practice

Prompt templating, token accounting and context windows, streaming and
cancellation, system-prompt design, and the operational metrics inherited
from @sec-sys-inference.

## Foundations

Why the surface works. Instruction tuning and RLHF as the training that
makes a completion model follow a chat contract, and the alignment between
the role structure and the conditional distribution the model represents.
